decisions.what: The zero-agent hold is now a MEASUREMENT rather than the conservative reading of an ambiguous posture that cycles 39 and 40 recorded. It also does not depend on KI-14 in either direction.
decisions.why: Cycles 39 and 40 held at zero agents because the allocator reported halted, then trickle-after-an-artefact-flip, and neither SKILL.md nor cycle.md defines the semantics (KI-13). That is a defensible reading but it is not evidence, and it left the run one bug-fix away from resuming spend for the wrong reason. This cycle transcribed bin/swarm-allocator.sh's calc() verbatim from its own constants (B0=90, floor=12, release=6h, lines 23-26 and 83-96) and reproduced the reported reserve to within 0.03 as a control (24.01 computed against 24.04 reported, the gap being the 3-minute clock difference since the allocator last refreshed). The result: allow_overall_pct is 0 because the human reserve (24.01) EXCEEDS the entire weekly remainder (100 - 93 = 7), and it is structurally 0 through stop_at -- the reserve floor releases only within 6h of the week reset and there are 17.59h left at stop_at, so it never releases during this run, while allow > 0 would need weekly_used_pct to FALL below 79.83%, which cannot happen because weekly usage is monotonic within a week. THE PART THAT MATTERS FOR KI-14: the rollover-jitter bug wipes the trickle counter and re-authorises the halted -> trickle flip, but it grants no actual spend here, because the allowance is already 0 on the reserve curve, which the wipe does not touch. So this run's hold is not resting on a bug, and equally the bug is not being credited with a safety it does not provide. Evidence: runs/cycle-041-allocmath.js and its output in the journal.

decisions.what: I-6 was executed NOW rather than at WRAP_UP, contradicting its own filed notes ("Runs at WRAP_UP by design").
decisions.why: Two reasons, and the second is the load-bearing one. (1) At zero authorised agent burn, I-6 is the only admissible item on a board of seven -- every other todo (T-007, T-008, T-024, T-024b, T-032, T-039) needs a builder. It is also the highest-priority item at 9. (2) The shipped REPORT.md was the 2026-08-14 SMOKE run's report, untouched since 05:58 that morning and 40 cycles out of date: it claimed 1 cycle, 48 tests, and a known-issues list ending at KI-3. If this session had died before WRAP_UP, the human would have opened a document describing the wrong run entirely. Deferring the run's only human-facing deliverable to a step that may never execute is a bet the run does not need to take, and WRAP_UP can now refresh a delta rather than author from scratch. Recorded as a departure from a written item note rather than taken silently.

decisions.what: The gate for a CONDUCTOR-AUTHORED document was run in two arms with a negative control, because the standard protection -- the builder never saw the check -- is unavailable when the conductor writes both the document and its gate.
decisions.why: Every prior gate this run rested on the builder not having seen the check. Here there was no builder: I wrote REPORT.md and I wrote the gate, so "the gate passed" carries no information about independence and reading the prose would only confirm it reads well, which is exactly what a confabulated document also does. The substitute is the cycle-7/8 rule (docs are falsifiable exactly like code) plus an explicit negative control: extract every falsifiable claim as a LITERAL and re-measure it against the repo, then run the identical gate against the previous REPORT.md from git HEAD and require it to FAIL. ACCEPTANCE 13/13, NEGATIVE 0/13. Without the second arm, a gate that merely asserted "the report mentions the corpus" would have scored 13/13 while measuring nothing.

decisions.what: Three gate checks were RED on the first run. Two were TRUE DEFECTS IN THE REPORT and were fixed in the document; one was the instrument measuring its own footprint and was fixed in the harness. Both harness repairs demand strictly more than v1 did.
decisions.why: Recorded with the split made explicit because cycles 19, 23 and 24 all found the INSTRUMENT at fault and a fourth such entry would wrongly suggest the same story. C8 was a real acceptance breach: I-4, the umbrella item, was absent from the I-item table, and I-6's acceptance says EVERY I-item. C10 was a real overclaim: the report graded KI-1 medium, but this run's state.json known_issues start at KI-2 -- KI-1 was resolved in the 2026-08-14 run and never carried forward, so the grade rested on a file the report does not cite. Both were fixed in REPORT.md (an I-4 umbrella row; an explicit provenance label on KI-1). C7 was the instrument: it asserted a raw ls|wc -l of .swarm/runs, which the gate increments by writing its own artifacts into that directory while it runs. v2 counts only cycles 1-40 and additionally REQUIRES the report to disclose the exclusion, and C10 v2 does not drop KI-1 from scrutiny but demands a provenance label v1 would not have required even on a matching severity. Neither repair could be motivated by a result it wanted to change: C8 and C10 were fixed in the document, not in the gate.

decisions.what: RETRO.md was pre-drafted at cycle 42 instead of at WRAP_UP, and on opening it the file turned out to be the 2026-08-14 SMOKE run's retro -- the IDENTICAL staleness defect cycle 41 found in REPORT.md, in the identical place, 4424 bytes untouched since 05:44 on 2026-08-14.
decisions.why: Same reasoning as cycle 41, now with a second confirming instance: a session death before WRAP_UP would hand the human a document describing the WRONG run, and BOTH of this run's human-facing deliverables were sitting in exactly that state. The generalisation worth carrying is that WRAP_UP-authored artifacts are the ones most exposed to session death, because they are written in the window where the run is least likely to get another cycle -- so the artifacts WRAP_UP owns should be drafted early and refreshed at WRAP_UP, not authored there. Recorded as a departure from the WRAP_UP-step-2a schedule rather than taken silently.

decisions.what: Five gate checks were RED on the first run. FOUR were genuine defects in the document and were fixed there; ONE was the instrument measuring a moving target. A sixth defect -- a check that PASSED vacuously -- was found only because a different check failed.
decisions.why: The split is the point, and it runs the opposite way from cycles 19/23/24, where the instrument was at fault. Document defects: (C8) cited week_resets_at as 1786942800, the cycle-41 harness's jitter-adjusted value, where the allocator itself reports 1786942799; (C10) named KI-1, which is absent from this run's state.json, with no provenance label; (C11) counted L-033 among the applied lessons when it is NOT in runfile.playbook.applied -- an inflation of the run's own playbook coverage; (C14) claimed 11 chartered must-haves where the board carries 12, the dropped one being I-4, the umbrella, which is the SAME omission cycle 41 found in REPORT.md. Instrument defect: (C9) required the document to contain the live-computed reserve as a frozen literal, but that value falls continuously with the week clock -- 24.01 at cycle 41, 23.60 during this cycle -- so it would go red on a CORRECT retro minutes later. The vacuous pass: C12 checked only that the applied-lessons tally SUMS to 15, and the first draft's wrong split 6/1/8 sums to 15 exactly as the true split 5/1/9 does. It passed a false tally and was caught only because C11 independently flagged the L-033 inflation that caused it.

decisions.what: The C10 instrument repair is recorded as a RELAXATION with its reason, not dressed up as a strengthening. Its sibling repairs (C9, C12) are strengthenings and are labelled separately.
decisions.why: Every prior harness repair this run could honestly claim to demand strictly more than the version it replaced, and there is a standing temptation to preserve that streak by framing. C10 v2 does two things in OPPOSITE directions: (a) it checks EVERY severity the document grades instead of three hardcoded ids, which is strictly stricter; (b) it admits an id absent from state.json when the document carries an explicit source-run provenance label, which is strictly weaker than v1's blanket refusal. (b) is a real relaxation, taken because v1 forbade a TRUE historical statement -- KI-1 was resolved in the 2026-08-14 run and never carried forward, and the cycle-41 finding about it is exactly the kind of thing a retro should be able to say. Calling that a strengthening would be the small dishonesty that makes the next one easier. C9 v2 and C12 v2 genuinely demand more: C9 now re-runs the arithmetic live and checks allow==0 at both endpoints plus the transcription control, none of which v1 did; C12 now counts the written verdicts instead of summing three numbers.

decisions.what: Playbook lesson L-008 (the conductor is the SOLE committer -- never commit or push yourself) is recorded as CONTRADICTED IN TEXT and upheld in spirit, on measured git evidence: three two-parent merge commits (b47d0e0, 73604d3, d737296) at cycles 15/16/17 each have a BUILDER-authored side parent, despite the directive being staged in every builder prompt.
decisions.why: The run's only measured contradiction of an applied lesson, and it was found by CHECKING rather than by remembering -- the RETRO draft asserted the lesson held, and the git history says otherwise. It matters because the directive's TEXT is stricter than its RATIONALE: the lesson was learned from parallel agents colliding on a SHARED tree, and a builder committing to its own disjoint branch which the conductor then merges sequentially, running the suite after each merge, is the documented build-wave design rather than a violation. No harm followed here. From cycle 18 on, KI-6 made /tmp worktrees unreachable and builders wrote directly into the shared tree -- the case the lesson is actually about -- and the conductor was sole committer for all 24 remaining cycles. Carried to the RETRO as a recommendation to SCOPE the directive to shared-tree dispatch, not to drop it. Note also the identity trap that made this checkable only by structure: every one of the 96 commits is authored 'SWARM', so authorship cannot distinguish a builder commit from a conductor commit -- only the merge parentage can.

decisions.what: The run is measured as NEITHER done NOR stalled, and the distinction is recorded rather than left implicit: definition-of-done IS met (all six improvement must-haves closed and conductor-verified, gate S3) while the target is NOT done, because T-008 still passes the value ratchet on a measured user-visible defect.
decisions.why: cycle.md churn breaker makes DONE a two-part test -- definition-of-done met AND no remaining candidate passing the ratchet -- and it would have been easy, and wrong, to read the first half as the whole test and declare the target done six hours early. Declaring DONE would have routed this run to an early WRAP_UP, disarmed the pacer, and told the human the product was finished when a corpus of 50 gives a repeat by use ~9.6. The opposite error was equally available: reading twelve item-less cycles as a stall. Neither holds (S9, S10), so the run continues to the clock. Recorded because both errors are attractive at 05:00 with an empty allowance, and both are visible only if the two-part test is applied literally.

decisions.what: CORRECTION to a claim this run repeated at cycles 41, 42 and 43 -- that all six remaining todos need a builder because the allowance is 0. Measured per item: three of the six are S-effort, which gear 1 explicitly admits. The gear is not their binding constraint; the cycle-39 family decision (T-024b, T-032) and T-039 own filing terms are.
decisions.why: The two constraints imply DIFFERENT human actions, and the conflated version implies the wrong one. "The allowance is 0" invites the inference that a healthier window restarts the whole board; for the three S-effort items it does not -- they are fenced by a measured decision that a seventh narrowing of the prose-anchored README guards costs more than it buys, and they unfence only when the M-effort T-024 umbrella lands or a BOUNDARY is argued. The tempting alternative — re-rank the board by what I think matters — would have produced the same top-two ordering and proven nothing. Both ordering checks carry a negative control that re-runs the identical predicate against the pre-edit snapshot and requires it to go RED (A2n, A3n), which is what separates a repair from a restatement.

decisions.what: The 12/12 first-run green was NOT the finding, and the finding did not come from the gate at all - it came from a THIRD instrument (cycle-050-suite-survivors.mjs) asking a question the gate does not ask: does the project's own suite catch the defects this gate catches?

decisions.what: M1 (unseeded off-by-one) and M3 (front bias) classified HOLE, not BOUNDARY - so T-043 is admitted as a hardening item under SPEC I-2 rather than documented and closed. M5 (seed-fold collapse) is NOT a survivor and is recorded as already protected.
decisions.why: SPEC I-2's classification turns on whether a stated rule exists that the mutant violates, and the Domain rules say plainly 'without --seed, selection is uniform over the filtered candidate set'. An off-by-one that makes the last corpus entry unreachable forever and a u->u^2 front bias both violate that rule outright, so this is not the cycle-4 M16 situation where writing a test would silently promote today's implementation to a promise - the promise is already written and simply unprotected. Recorded alongside its opposite: M5 leaves --seed perfectly deterministic while making it useless, and had it survived it would have been the harder call, because no rule promises seed SURJECTIVITY. It did not survive, so that call does not have to be made and is not made here.

decisions.what: T-043 filed as a BACKLOG ITEM, not a known_issue, with an explicit standing instruction that WRAP_UP must promote it to a known_issue if it has not landed by then.

Filing it as a KI now would over-count the hand-off's open-issue tally for a thing about to close; leaving it as a quietly unworked board item at stop_at would under-report it. decisions.what: The corpus-size arithmetic was put in REPORT.md as a decision FRAME for T-008 rather than as a recommendation, even though it argues fairly directly for a feature this run's non-goals fence out.

Deferred because WRAP_UP is ~85 minutes out and produces a STRICT SUPERSET of what a recycle note produces: REPORT.md, RETRO.md, the distilled playbook candidates and a final journal block all re-orient a fresh session from disk, where a handoff note only re-orients. decisions.what: The uniformity test asserts REACHABILITY and EQUAL SHARE, both order-agnostic — it deliberately does NOT pin which u maps to which candidate, and the gate s decisive check is a reversed-but-uniform rewrite that must stay GREEN.
decisions.why: Every acceptance-shaped check asks whether a VIOLATING implementation is caught, and a guard that simply froze today s arithmetic (u -> floor(u*n), this exact mapping) catches both cycle-50 survivors too. The two readings only separate on an implementation that is uniform but mapped differently. That is not hypothetical: the Domain rule promises uniformity over the candidate set and says nothing about ordering, so walking the candidates in reverse honours it exactly, and a mapping-pinned guard would fire on a CORRECT rewrite — a false rejection a maintainer resolves by deleting the guard, which is worse than never having written it. So the probe was run: index = n-1-floor(u*n) leaves the suite at 82/0. This is the cycle-21/22 consistent-change method transplanted from documents to an algorithm — change the thing under test in a way that keeps the RULE true, and require green.

decisions.what: DISCLOSED WEAKNESS IN THIS CYCLE S EVIDENCE: the conductor wrote both the test and the gate that judges it, so hard rule 2 s central protection — the builder never saw the check — does not apply to T-043.
decisions.why: The allocator authorises zero agent burn (fourth consecutive REAL probe at allow 0), so there was no builder to keep blind. Recording it rather than letting a 7/7 gate imply a separation that did not exist. What carries the result instead, and is weaker than the usual arrangement but is not nothing: both mutants are PRE-REGISTERED — they were measured as survivors at cycle 50, before this test was conceived, and their text is copied verbatim from that harness rather than authored alongside the test. The attribution arms (R1 strict, R2 denominator) are measurements whose outcome the author does not control. The genuinely unprotected direction is the one no pre-registration fixes: a hole this test does not cover would not be found by its own author. That is why check D exists and why the item s notes state per-test kill attribution rather than a combined figure.

decisions.what: Honest per-test accounting recorded rather than a combined kill figure: M1 is killed by both new tests, M3 by the EQUAL-SPLIT test alone. The REACHABILITY test is silent on M3.
decisions.why: Under u -> u**2 every index remains reachable — the front bias changes the SHARES, not the support — so the reachability test cannot see it, and the gate output shows exactly that (M3: 81 pass / 1 fail). The tempting summary, two tests kill two mutants, would double-count what this cycle bought. Cycle 23 set this rule when T-017 s binary-side kills turned out to belong to a pre-existing test; the same discipline applies when the overlap runs the other way.

decisions.what: The coverage sweep's own instrument was defective on its first two passes, and BOTH defects were caught by the sweep's controls rather than by review. Recorded as a finding, not a footnote.
decisions.why: Pass 1 reported S4 (front-bias mutant) as INERT — meaning 'the mutation had no observable effect'. That was FALSE and it was my arithmetic: under index = floor(r**2 * n) the back-half share is P(r > sqrt(0.5)) = 0.293, not 0, and the witness threshold (>=30 of 120 draws) is one the MUTANT clears at ~35. The witness could not separate uniform from biased, so INERT was a verdict about the instrument. Re-powered to 400 draws with a threshold of 160 (~4 sd below uniform, ~4.8 sd above the mutant); S4 then read KILLED. Passes 1 and 2 also resolved ZERO test names on 25 kills: both anchored on a TAP `not ok` line that this runner never emits — `node --test` defaults to the SPEC reporter here (`✖ <name> (<n>ms)`), and the pass/fail counts only ever parsed because the inherited cycle-50 regex leads with a wildcard char that happens to match the spec reporter's `ℹ`. This is exactly the pattern KI-19 named one cycle earlier — a hand-written per-cycle script inheriting the previous script's blind spots — and it is the first time that pattern has been caught INSIDE the cycle that committed it. IMPORTANT, because the obvious inference is wrong: cycle 51's gate is NOT affected. Its runner passed `--test-reporter=tap` explicitly, so its regexes matched its own invocation, and it carried an `unparseable` guard that would have failed the cell rather than silently returning empty names. Its 7/7 stands. The defect is mine: I inherited cycle 50's runner (no TAP flag) alongside cycle 51's TAP-shaped parser.

known_issues.desc: Subagents in this VPS -p session are sandboxed to the session --add-dir list (/opt/swarm, /opt/targets/aphorism-cli). A git worktree under /tmp is therefore UNREACHABLE to a builder: reads, bash, and EnterWorktree all refuse. Cycle 18 lost one builder dispatch to this. SKILL.md already prescribes "no worktrees" for headless sessions and gives disjoint file scopes as the concurrency answer instead; cycles 16-17 used /tmp worktrees anyway and cycle 18 is where it bit. Remedy for future cycles: at k_cap 1 let the single builder work directly in the target tree (conductor still sole committer); for k>1 headless, either scope builders to disjoint files in the one tree or place worktrees INSIDE an allowed directory.

Subagent scratch files land in the SWARM root (/opt/swarm) unless the dispatch prompt names an explicit scratch path. Hard rule 5 hands agents target paths only, but the session cwd IS /opt/swarm, so a relative scratch path silently lands inside the write fence -- the fence is enforced by what agents are TOLD, and cwd supplies what they were not told. Observed cycle 9 (builder used /opt/swarm/.scratch/) and again at cycles 17-18 (9 untracked .js/.json scratch files in the SWARM root, removed by the conductor at cycle 19). Harmless so far -- all occurrences were inert scratch, nothing under bin/, reference/, workflows/ or templates/ -- but the same reflex on a different task could write into SWARM tooling mid-run. CYCLE 36: control PASSES a third consecutive time. The dispatch prompt named an explicit scratch path (<target>/.swarm/scratch-c36/) and the builder used it; /opt/swarm stayed clean, verified by `git -C /opt/swarm status --porcelain`. The builder did NOT remove its own scratch tree this time (cycle 35's did), so the conductor removed it before commit -- the naming control is what is working; self-cleanup is not reliable and should not be assumed.
known_issues.note_cycle_21: THIRD occurrence, in a new and milder variant: the dispatch prompt named the explicit in-target scratch path as the remedy prescribes, and the builder honored it AND deleted its mutation copies -- but left the bare empty .swarm/scratch directory behind. Measured at 0 files inside, so nothing leaked and no untracked scratch reached git status; this is the same residue cycle 9 recorded (agent removes copies, conductor removes the empty directory). Caught only because the conductor gate carries a standing SCOPE.SCRATCH control, which is the reason to keep that control even on cycles where it looks like a formality. Remedy refinement for the wrap-up distillation: the prompt should say remove the scratch DIRECTORY, not just its contents.
known_issues.remedy: Name an explicit scratch directory in every dispatch prompt. NOT /tmp -- KI-6 established subagents are sandboxed to the session --add-dir list, so /tmp is unreachable. Use <target>/.swarm/scratch/ and require the agent to remove it, with a conductor gate check confirming the removal. Done this way at cycle 19 (T-013) and the agent left nothing behind (harness controls CTRL-SCRATCH, CTRL-TREE). known_issues.note_cycle_24: FOURTH occurrence, and it PARTIALLY CONTRADICTS the cycle-22 note below, so that note should not be read on its own. The cycle-21 remedy refinement was again applied verbatim in the dispatch prompt -- it named the in-target scratch path AND required removing the scratch DIRECTORY itself, not merely its contents, calling out that an empty directory counts as debris and is checked. The builder created three subdirectories under .swarm/scratch/ and reported removing them with rm -rf, which it had genuinely done: the standing SCOPE.SCRATCH control found .swarm/scratch present with ZERO entries inside. So the agent removed what it created and still left the parent it did not create. Nothing leaked, git status showed no untracked scratch, and the conductor removed the directory by hand. The lesson for the wrap-up distillation is narrower and more useful than 'name the scratch path': an agent told to remove its scratch directory removes the directories IT MADE, so the prompt must name the exact path whose absence is checked, or the check must tolerate an empty parent.
